content: Uterine fibroids are known to cause symptoms such as heavy and prolonged menstrual bleeding, pelvic pain, pressure-related symptoms, and subfertility. Historically, surgical interventions have been the primary treatment option, as medical therapies have not demonstrated sufficient efficacy. Uterine artery embolization (UAE) has emerged as a minimally invasive alternative for women who do not wish to preserve fertility. This review evaluates the benefits and risks of UAE compared to other medical or surgical treatments for symptomatic uterine fibroids. The review included seven randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 793 women. Three trials compared UAE with abdominal hysterectomy, two compared UAE with myomectomy, and two compared UAE with either hysterectomy or myomectomy. Patient satisfaction rates within 24 months of the procedure showed no clear difference between UAE and surgery, with satisfaction rates potentially being up to 41% lower or 48% higher with UAE (odds ratio [OR] 0.94; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.59 to 1.48). Similarly, findings at five years post-procedure were inconclusive (OR 0.90; 95% CI 0.45 to 1.80). The quality of evidence for these outcomes was moderate. Regarding fertility outcomes, there was very low-quality evidence from a single study suggesting that myomectomy may result in better fertility outcomes than UAE. Specifically, the odds of live birth were lower with UAE (OR 0.26; 95% CI 0.08 to 0.84), as were the odds of pregnancy (OR 0.29; 95% CI 0.10 to 0.85). However, these findings should be interpreted with caution due to the limited and low-quality data. In terms of safety, there was no clear evidence of a difference in the risk of major complications between UAE and surgery, either during the procedure (OR 0.91; 95% CI 0.42 to 1.97) or within one year (OR 0.65; 95% CI 0.33 to 1.26) or five years (OR 0.56; 95% CI 0.27 to 1.18) post-procedure. However, UAE was associated with a higher rate of minor complications within one year (OR 1.99; 95% CI 1.41 to 2.81) and up to five years (OR 2.93; 95% CI 1.73 to 4.93). The quality of evidence for these safety outcomes ranged from low to moderate. UAE was also associated with a significantly higher likelihood of requiring additional surgical interventions within two to five years of the initial procedure. Within two years, the odds of requiring further surgery were higher with UAE (OR 3.72; 95% CI 2.28 to 6.04), and this increased further at five years (OR 5.79; 95% CI 2.65 to 12.65). If 7% of women undergoing hysterectomy or myomectomy require further surgery within two years, this figure rises to between 15% and 32% for women undergoing UAE. On the other hand, UAE was associated with several procedural advantages. Women undergoing UAE were less likely to require a blood transfusion compared to those undergoing surgery (OR 0.07; 95% CI 0.01 to 0.52). Additionally, UAE was linked to shorter procedural times, reduced hospital stays, and faster resumption of normal activities. However, these outcomes could not be pooled due to variability between studies. The quality of evidence varied across outcomes, with moderate-quality evidence for satisfaction rates and most safety outcomes, but very low-quality evidence for fertility outcomes. Limitations in the evidence included wide confidence intervals, unclear reporting of methods, and lack of blinding for subjective outcomes. In conclusion, there is no clear difference in patient satisfaction between UAE and surgery within two years of the procedure, and findings at five years remain inconclusive. While UAE is a safe and minimally invasive alternative to surgery, it is associated with a higher rate of minor complications and a significantly increased likelihood of requiring further surgical intervention within two to five years. This higher re-intervention rate may offset the initial cost advantages of UAE. Patient selection and thorough counselling are critical to ensure appropriate treatment decisions.
